senses: The property of being livable.
examples: The livability of the shack was questioned, but the old man had lived there for 50 years.

senses: Grinning; having happiness or satisfaction apparent on one's face.
A pastry consisting of a filling (typically fruit or cheese) inside a bread roll, popular in the United States.
ety: Borrowed from Czech koláče and Slovak koláče, plural of koláč. Doublet of kalach and kolach.

senses: Any long slender primitive eel-like freshwater and saltwater fish of the order Petromyzontiformes, having a sucking mouth with rasping teeth but no jaw.
ety: From Middle English laumprei, from Old French lampreie (modern French lamproie), from Medieval Latin lampreda, possibly alteration of Late Latin lampetra (“lamprey”), whose further origin is unknown, though it is traditionally thought to be a combination of lambō (“to lick, lap”) + petra (“stone, rock”). Doublet of limpet, which derives from Latin.

senses: Having a single color.
Capable of being frozen; especially capable of use after subsequent thawing.
A flash of light; a spark.
The flash of light produced by something (especially a phosphor) when it absorbs ionizing radiation.
A brief expression that is amusing or clever; witticism.
A round metal platter used to serve food in India.
A meal served on such a platter, typically comprising a selection of different dishes presented in small bowls.
examples: In front of it was a gold thali filled to overflowing with all manner of food, most of it sweets and pastries made from milk and curds.

senses: A Eurasian blackbird (Turdus merula).
A water ouzel, an aquatic perching bird (Cinclus mexicanus).
ety: From Middle English osel, from Old English ōsle, from Proto-West Germanic *ą̄slā, *amslā, from Proto-Germanic *amslǭ. Cognate with German Amsel. For the spelling, compare Early Modern English bloud (“blood”).

senses: A person involved in the labour movement.
The official currency of Nigeria. Equal to 100 kobo. (The naira replaced the pound in 1973.)
ety: A contraction of Nigeria, coined by Federal Commissioner for Finance Obafemi Awolowo.

senses: The behaviour of a clown; clownishness, tomfoolery.
examples: Defensive clownery by the Mets at certain points of the game ultimately cost the 22-year-old Niese his first major league win in eight months.

senses: Having the ability to produce a tornado.
That enhances physical performance (especially in sports or exercise).
A branch of zoology that studies fish.
That celebrates or commemorates a triumph or victory.
ety: From Middle English triumphal, triumphall, tryumphal, from Latin triumphālis and Old French trionfal, triumphal.

senses: A member of Nigeria's National Youth Service Corps.
examples: I have wanted to leave since the three corpers in the National Youth Service programme were killed.

senses: An ornate capital letter used in calligraphy, consisting of interlaced pen strokes. See :Commons:Cadel letters.
ety: From Latin capitellum, diminuitive of Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of captain. Cognate with French cadeau. Doublet of caddie, cadet, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

senses: A horse or human athlete who participates in steeplechase racing
examples: Tasmanian steeplechaser Donna MacFarlane opens her 2009 campaign over 1500m in a tough clash with Beijing Games teammate Corrigan.

senses: Collectively, the mechanisms of a woodwind musical instrument such as a flute or clarinet that support the operation of its keys.
The form of social work done by a keyworker.
examples: The fingering challenges that arise are similar to those above, involving unorthodox key usage, half- and sometimes quarter-holing, and unusual configurations of keywork.

senses: A ruff worn during the beginning of the 17th century; a cope.
A high-quality grade of Spanish saffron.
The development and production of new vaccines.
That damages or destroys cells
Of, similar to, or related to paper.
The theory of poetry, or of literature in general.
A motor-driven logging machine which transports logs by means of a system of cables and winches.
A painter who paints watercolors.
A person who subscribes to situationism.
examples: In 1976 and 1977, and the years to follow, as symbolically remade by the Sex Pistols, it was, perhaps, dadaists, lettrists, situationists, and various medieval heretics.

senses: A construction material consisting of a rigid panel of several layers of fibreboard or paper bonded to a gypsum core.
Resembling or characteristic of a lamb or the meat of a lamb.
examples: We try to avoid a lamby or "woolly" flavor.
The resulting sausages, incorporated into various dishes or grilled on their own, are plump torpedoes of lamby goodness, aggressively and expertly spiced.
Méchoui is like a foretaste of paradise, the tenderest and most delicious meat surrounded by the crispest, lambiest skin imaginable.

senses: An agent that prevents or counteracts malaria.
A mulching mower.
An ancient Roman official responsible for public revenue and other financial affairs.
The Quaestor sacri palatii of the late Roman Empire and Byzantium; first generally a legislator, then judicial official, and eventually an honorary title by the 14th century.
In the Middle Ages, an officer who announced indulgences.
ety: From Middle English questor, from Latin quaestor, from an old participle form of quaerō.

senses: The interdisciplinary study of literature and ecology.
examples: A chapter on North Woods writers is an ideal project in which to engage the fundamental issues of ecocriticism.
In this light, the current volume is a work of ecocriticism, although not all the contributors would wish to define themselves first and foremost as ecocritics.
Serpil Opperman writes that ecocriticism proposes “that we can read the world as matter endowed with stories.”

senses: To cause (an animal) to excrete any worms in the digestive tract by the administration of drugs.
examples: Hey, Ethel, you know it's your turn to deworm the cat?

senses: Someone who terrorizes, who induces terror, a terror.
Between the eyes.
Not killable; unable to be killed.
Like a nook; small and secluded or cosy.
examples: And so you will find that his whole orchard is a quaint and nooky place where one may not only pick apples, but may saunter and rest.
